newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi says local polls back Italy's economic efforts.
newsitem.headline: Prodi says local polls back Italy's economic efforts.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi said on Wednesday results of weekend local elections showed Italians understood the need to make economic sacrifices for the country's future.

"To a large extent the people have understood the need for their own sacrifices and our efforts. The electoral result is very clear on this point: They have not rejected us," Prodi said in an interview with the daily La Stampa newspaper.

Italy has imposed a hefty dose of economic belt-tightening through a budget and mini-budget in the past year to cut the country's budget deficit to help Italy qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Prodi said that the first-round results of Sunday's elections in more than 1,100 cities and towns had strengthened his ruling centre-left coalition despite a poor showing in the two big northern cities of Milan and Turin.
"There is a problem...for the centre-left in two cities as undeniably important as Milan and Turin," he said, "I will not try to hide that."

Prodi said the two major industrial centres were dominated by that section of society most hit by the financial measures enacted by the government in its effort to ensure that Italy qualifies for the single currency from the outset in 1999.

The first round results showed that the hard-left Communist Refoundation, which secures Prodi's majority in the lower house of parliament but does not hold any posts in government, did particularly well in the provinces.

Prodi shrugged off suggestions that the coalition would be pulled more to the left as a result of Refoundation's success by saying the data did not give them added weight and other parties of the centre-left had also done well.
"As far as Refoundation is concerned, they have maintained their share of the vote, a point more and a point less. They fell in the cities, grew in the provinces."
Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni told the daily Corriere della Sera that the centre-left had won the elections and there was no alternative to the government.
